title: Security evaluation of quantum distance-bounding protocols via semidefinite programming
authors: Kevin Bogner, Aysajan Abidin, Dave Singelee, Bart Preneel
abstract: Quantum distance-bounding (QDB) protocols let a verifier check that a prover is both genuine and physically nearby. During a timed fast phase of quantum communication, the verifier measures round-trip times to obtain an upper bound on the prover's distance. For a uniform comparison, we isolate the fast phase and study one-round distance-fraud (DF) and mafia-fraud (MF) games. For discrete-variable QDB, we show that these games reduce to convex optimization problems and can therefore be solved exactly with semidefinite programming; each MF value comes with an explicit attack achieving it and a matching certificate that no attack does better. This contrasts with quantum position verification, where an attack is split between two separated parties, so its optimization is nonconvex and analyses rely on relaxations. In our MF game, the cooperating pair collapses to a single sequential strategy, which keeps the game convex and its exact value computable. Across the discrete-variable protocols we examine, the best one-round DF attack succeeds with the same probability ($1/2$) for every protocol, whereas MF clearly separates the protocols. For continuous-variable QDB, we report estimated attack success probabilities from a calibrated Gaussian attack model. The benchmark covers protocols whose fast phase itself authenticates the prover; designs that follow Brands and Chaum and instead bind the fast phase with a final authenticated message, like the earliest QDB proposal, fall outside it and are treated separately. Of the four protocols studied, two had no previously known one-round attack values, and we report the first ones; for the other two, we find MF attacks with higher success probability than previously reported. Overall, one-round MF resistance depends on whether an attacker can use information revealed early by the prover to answer a fresh challenge from the verifier.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the security of Quantum Distance-Bounding protocols by modeling them as one-round fraud games. Using Semidefinite Programming, they compute exact attack success probabilities for discrete variables, demonstrating that Mafia-Fraud resistance can distinguish between different QDB designs. This work advances the theoretical understanding of physical distance verification in quantum communication.
main_problem: The paper evaluates the security of Quantum Distance-Bounding (QDB) protocols by isolating and studying one-round distance-fraud (DF) and mafia-fraud (MF) games.
main_result: For discrete variables, SDPs allow for exact computation of MF attack values, showing that MF clearly separates studied QDB protocols. The overall resistance depends on whether an attacker can use early information to answer fresh challenges.
method: The authors reduce the one-round DF and MF games to convex optimization problems solvable exactly using Semidefinite Programming (SDP) for discrete variables, while employing calibrated Gaussian models for continuous variables.
model_or_system: The study focuses on QDB protocols that use timed quantum communication in a fast phase to bound physical distance. The analysis covers both discrete-variable and continuous-variable constructions.
key_observables: Success probability of the best single-round attack ($p_\star^{MF}$ or $p_\star^{DF}$) for various QDB protocols.
important_parameters: The one-round nature of the fast phase, which simplifies the optimization problem compared to full quantum position verification.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to a single round; for continuous variables, it uses a finite-grid approximation due to intractable non-convexity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the flow diagrams of specific QDB protocols (e.g., QDB 2017, E91 QDB) detailing verifier/prover actions across multiple rounds.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the framework by isolating one-round games; it then details the SDP formulation for discrete variables and Gaussian estimation for continuous variables, presenting results via tables comparing calculated attack values to prior work.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous mathematical tools (SDP) to analyze security bounds in quantum communication protocols, which is foundational knowledge for quantum cryptography and secure quantum networking.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reduced mafia-fraud SDP game. The adversary’s comb S first interacts with the prover via the pre-ask channel Nω, then answers the verifier’s challenge ρω. The branch-dependent triple (Nω, ρω, Πω), with Πω the verifier’s accept operator, combines into a single tester operator Wω that captures everything outside the adversary’s control on branch ω. The acceptance probability is then Tr(WωS), a linear function of the comb S; this linearity is what makes the optimization an SDP.

Figure 2: CV-QDB calibration sweeps with zero added response noise σ2 resp = 0. Panel (a) varies the threshold at fixed rsq = 1.2, while panel (b) varies the squeezing at fixed δcv = 1.1. Mafia-fraud values are finite-grid Gaussian estimators recomputed for each parameter point. Black outlines identify the calibrated operating point used in Table 1.

Figure 3: Overview of the QDB 2017 protocol [AMSP17]. Before the fast rounds, the parties exchange nonces and derive the PRF output a. In each fast round, the verifier prepares |ci⟩ai, and the prover measures it in basis ai and re-prepares the outcome in the same basis. After all rounds, the prover sends τ = MACx(IDV, IDP, Nv, Np, cP ). The verifier accepts only if τ equals the MAC recomputed on cV , all recovered bits match the originals, and every round-trip time ∆ti stays below tmax.

Figure 4: Overview of the QDB 2019 protocol [Abi19]. Before the fast rounds, the parties exchange nonces and derive the PRF outputs a and b. In each fast round, the verifier prepares |ci⟩ai, and the prover measures it in basis ai and re-prepares the outcome in basis bi. After all rounds, the verifier accepts only if all recovered bits match the originals and every round-trip time ∆ti stays below tmax.

Figure 5: Overview of the Mutual QDB protocol [AES25]. Before the fast rounds, the parties exchange nonces and derive the PRF outputs a, b, and γ, and the prover commits to a random mask string r. In each fast round, the verifier prepares an EPR pair, measures its own half in basis ai, and sends the prover half EPp,i. The prover measures in the same basis and returns |m′ i ⊕ri⟩bi. The verifier then recovers the mask bit and sends back |r′ i⟩γi. After all rounds, the prover opens the commitment and reveals m′.
